idea: The core problem is that meaning is tangled and hard to pin down. How do you know whether one user's taste matches another, or whether one product is like another, or whether two scientific claims are about the same thing? Instead of trying to write down rules that capture meaning (which always fails—context matters, people disagree, exceptions proliferate), a radically different approach emerged: find a high-dimensional space and arrange every item in it so that things humans treat as alike end up at similar coordinates. Once you have such a space, the nebulous question 'what is like this?' becomes the mechanical question 'what is close by in the space?'—and distance is something you can compute, compare, and optimize. The genius is that you don't need to know *why* two things are alike; you only need enough data about which pairs humans put together, and you can learn a space where that data comes true. Meaning becomes geometry.
why: This works because the high-dimensional space is expressive enough to capture *relationships* without having to enumerate them. A user's taste for comedy films, their comfort with subtitles, their budget constraints—these don't need separate logic; they all become different directions through the space, and each one automatically finds its own axis of variation. The deeper mechanism: when the space is learned well, most of the real signal concentrates into just a few directions (the principal structure), leaving most dimensions as noise. This is why you can build trustworthy systems: if two users sit close in the space, it's not by accident—it means their choices cluster the same way across the dimensions that *actually matter*. The cost comes when the underlying pattern is genuinely high-dimensional or when the space is learned from weak signals; then 'close in space' can be meaningless. The power persists because high-dimensional spaces are surprisingly friendly: two random points are almost never close (the 'curse of dimensionality' becomes an asset), so when closeness appears, it usually signals real structure.
dots: Across the 302 papers, this thread appears in constantly shifting disguises. In recommendation (ARCHER, Learning on Adaptive Manifolds), the space is user-item taste—images and text descriptions of products get mapped to a shared coordinate system where clicking patterns and visual similarity agree. In classification (Language Model Representations for Few-Shot Tabular), unknown tables become points in semantic space, with distances encoding what kind of rows they are. In graph problems (C-HyPOD, Node Role-Guided LLMs), the space uses curved geometry to naturally capture hierarchies—closeness in curved space encodes both type relationships and structural roles. Information retrieval papers (LongRanker, CiteLLM, OwlerLite) place documents and queries in the same space and rank by distance. Cross-modal retrieval (HL-CMR, MCoT-MVS, Multi-view Semantic Contrastive Alignment) stretches one space across images, text, and user behavior, forcing all three modalities to agree on which items sit together. Even diffusion processes (Conditional Diffusion Guided Knowledge Transfer) and temporal forecasting (Efficient High-Dimensional Time Series Forecasting) follow the same recipe: arrange time steps or latent states in space so that causally related ones bunch together. The unifying move is always the same: pick a meaningful space, define what 'close' means in it, and let the distance metric do the work that rules would require.
picture: Imagine you're organizing a library without an index. Instead of labeling shelves, you physically rearrange books so that readers naturally find similar titles by walking in the right direction—biographies cluster near each other, and if you move toward them from fiction, the fiction nearest to biography (historical novels) sits on the border. A reader asking 'what else is like this?' no longer needs a librarian; they just look left or right. The surprising part: the shelving layout isn't decided by genre labels handed down from publishing; it emerges from watching which books readers pick up together. The space—the physical arrangement—is learned from behavior, not invented ahead of time.
